opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

From my experience, the first priority, and by far the most important, is people. A research institute is only as good as the researchers in it. When we started, we didn't have a long track record or a famous brand in this part of the world, so the question was how to attract truly world-class talent and convince them to bet their careers on something new. That meant recruiting very selectively, keeping the bar high even when it would have been easier to grow faster, and investing heavily in young people: students, interns, and early-career researchers. Many of the people who later became leaders in academia and industry came through as very young researchers. If you get the talent right, almost everything else follows.

The second priority is culture. You need an environment that is open, that values curiosity, and that tolerates failure. Real research means most of your ideas won't work. If people are afraid to fail, they'll only pursue safe, incremental problems, and you'll never produce breakthroughs. So we tried to build a flat, collaborative culture where a junior researcher could challenge a senior one, and where the best idea wins regardless of who it came from.

Third is having the right balance between long-term research and real-world impact. A world-class lab has to publish at the top venues and push the frontier of science. That's how you earn credibility in the global community. But in a corporate setting you also need to transfer technology into products that touch hundreds of millions of people. I've always thought of these not as competing goals but as reinforcing each other. Hard real-world problems inspire better research, and good research creates new possibilities for products.

Fourth is openness to the global community. Science has no borders. We worked closely with universities, sent people to conferences, hosted visiting scholars, and supported students across the region. Being part of the international research ecosystem, rather than isolated from it, was essential.

And finally, patience. Building a great research institute takes years, even decades. You have to choose a few important directions, stay committed, and resist the temptation to chase every short-term trend. The return on fundamental research often comes much later than anyone expects, but when it comes, it can be transformative.

So if I had to summarize: talent, culture, the balance of research and impact, openness, and long-term commitment. Those are the foundations.

r001.rationale: It calls people the first and most important priority and describes selectively recruiting world-class talent.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing a few important research directions, staying committed for the long term, and notes that fundamental research can later have transformative returns.

r003.rationale: It describes investing in students and early-career researchers, with the aim of helping them grow into future leaders.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, thank you for having me. I've thought about this question a lot, because I've had the chance to be part of building a few institutions from the ground up, Microsoft Research Asia back in 1998, and more recently the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua. And honestly, the answer hasn't changed much over twenty-plus years.

The first priority, and really the only one that matters in the beginning, is people. Not buildings, not budget, not even the research agenda. You hire the very best people you can find, people who are better than you in their own domain, and then you give them enough freedom and enough resources that they would be embarrassed not to do great work. At MSR Asia, Kai-Fu Lee and I spent most of our first year just recruiting. We went to every top university, we called people in Silicon Valley who were doing well and asked them to take a chance on something that didn't exist yet. A world-class institute is really just a world-class group of people in the same place, with a culture that lets them trust each other.

The second thing is that you have to set the bar for ambition very high and very early. If the first ten people you hire are doing incremental work, the next hundred will too. So we were quite deliberate about saying, we're not here to localize products or do engineering support. We want to publish at the top venues, we want to influence the direction of the field, and we want some of the work to end up changing what the company ships. That dual mission, basic research and real impact, creates some tension, but I actually think the tension is healthy. It keeps the researchers honest about relevance and keeps the engineers honest about depth.

Third, you need a long time horizon and patience from whoever is funding you. Research doesn't deliver on a quarterly schedule. We were lucky that Bill Gates and Rick Rashid understood this. If leadership starts demanding a return in eighteen months, the culture bends toward safe projects and you lose the thing you were trying to build. So part of my job was always managing upward, protecting the space for people to fail a few times before they succeeded.

And the last thing I'd mention, which is maybe underappreciated, is openness. Publish, collaborate with universities, let people leave and go start companies or become professors. Early on some people worried this was giving away talent. But over time the alumni network became one of the institute's biggest assets. If you look at how many leaders in Chinese AI today came through MSR Asia, that openness is a large part of why the institute mattered, not just to Microsoft but to the whole ecosystem.

So, people first, high ambition, patience, and openness. Everything else, the org charts, the research directions, the metrics, those are downstream of getting those four right.

r001.rationale: It says the first priority is people and describes recruiting the very best researchers as the institute’s starting point.

r002.rationale: It calls for high ambition, field influence, and patience, but does not clearly say to choose research priorities based on their potential long-term impact.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes recruiting top people and giving them freedom and resources, but does not identify developing first-rate researchers as an institute goal.

astra-6.text:
I would put people first. A world-class research institute needs outstanding researchers, but it also needs an environment where they can do their best work—where they have intellectual freedom, strong colleagues, and the confidence to pursue ideas that may take years to mature.

Second, you need focus. You cannot lead in every area, so you have to choose a few important problems where you can make a distinctive contribution. And you need a balance between fundamental research and real-world impact. Practical problems can inspire very deep research, while fundamental advances can create opportunities nobody anticipated.

Third, the institute must be open: connected to universities, industry, and the international research community. You want ideas and talent moving across those boundaries.

Finally, leadership has to be patient. You should set high standards, but you cannot manage research entirely through quarterly milestones. The goal is to build a culture that consistently produces new knowledge and develops the next generation of research leaders.

r001.rationale: The response puts people first and says the institute needs outstanding researchers, but it does not identify recruiting first-rate talent as the initial priority.

r002.rationale: The response recommends focusing on a few important problems and balancing fundamental research with real-world impact, but it does not say to choose priorities for their potential long-term impact.

r003.rationale: It explicitly names developing the next generation of research leaders as a goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I would put people first. A world-class institute needs outstanding researchers, but it also needs an environment where they can do their best work—with intellectual freedom, strong support, and colleagues who challenge and inspire them.

Second, you need a clear research vision. You cannot lead in every area, so you have to choose a few important problems where you can make a distinctive contribution. There should be a balance between fundamental research with a long horizon and work that addresses real needs.

Third, you need an open culture: collaboration across disciplines, close relationships with universities and industry, and a commitment to developing young talent. Ultimately, I would judge an institute by the ideas it contributes, the people it develops, and the impact its work has.

r001.rationale: The response puts people first and says the institute needs outstanding researchers, but it does not identify recruiting them as the initial priority.

r002.rationale: It recommends balancing research on important problems with fundamental research that has a long horizon.

r003.rationale: It names developing young talent as a commitment and says an institute should be judged by the people it develops.
